issues.legal_issue: A ruler who retained sovereign authority could identify property as private property after the deadline for submitting an inventory when the governing covenant imposed no consequence for late submission.
material_facts: The covenant required rulers to submit inventories of private property before a specified deadline but contained no provision barring later submission or divesting title for a late inventory.
The ruler retained sovereign authority after integration except for the aspects surrendered or redistributed under the arrangements between the states.
After the inventory deadline, the ruler submitted a list identifying the disputed house as private property.
issues.conclusion: The ruler remained entitled to identify the house as private property after the inventory deadline, and the late submission did not divest his title.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article XI of the covenant, a ruler was to furnish an inventory of private property before the stated deadline, but the covenant provided no penalty or forfeiture for late submission. Article VI transferred rights and powers relating to the government of the state, while the ruler retained sovereignty except to the extent surrendered or redistributed. The Court relied on Virendra Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, which held that integration redistributed aspects of sovereignty but did not itself extinguish the rulers’ remaining sovereignty.

predicates.property_status_dispute_under_state_inte: The dispute concerns whether property was a ruler’s private property or state property under an arrangement integrating states.
predicates.ruler_retained_sovereign_authority: The ruler retained sovereign authority over matters not surrendered or redistributed by the integration arrangement.
predicates.inventory_deadline_passed: The deadline for submitting an inventory of private property had passed.
predicates.no_forfeiture_for_late_inventory: The governing arrangement did not provide that missing the inventory deadline would bar a later submission or forfeit title.
predicates.ruler_later_listed_property_as_private: After the deadline, the ruler submitted an inventory identifying the property as private.

issues.definition: When a property-status dispute arises under a state-integration arrangement, a ruler who retains sovereign authority and later lists property as private may do so after the inventory deadline if the arrangement does not impose forfeiture for late submission.

issues.legal_issue: A gift of property identified as a ruler’s private property remains effective against the state when the ruler had authority to make the gift and later administrative materials do not validly divest the recipient’s title.
material_facts: The ruler identified the house as private property in a list submitted after the inventory deadline.
The ruler made a written gift of the house after submitting that list, and the recipient possessed it when the state brought its suit.
The ruler denied receiving the later letter and lists on which the state relied to claim that the house had been classified as state property.

The Court found no direct evidence of the alleged conference and held that even if it occurred, its minutes did not divest the recipient of title; no dispute had been determined by the judicial officer contemplated by the governing arrangements.
The state’s suit sought possession and damages, and the High Court had granted relief to the state.
issues.conclusion: The gift was effective, the later letter and lists did not divest the recipient’s title, and the state’s claim for possession and damages failed.
issues.legal_principle: Article XI of the covenant and Article VII of the later agreement distinguished private property from state property and provided for disputes to be decided by a judicial officer nominated by the Government of India. Article VI transferred powers relating to administration of the state but did not authorize the ruler, after integration, to take private property from another person. Applying Virendra Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, the Court held that the ruler retained the relevant sovereignty when he identified the property and made the gift. The later letter and lists did not establish a valid divestiture, and the claimed administrative conference could not replace the prescribed determination of a property dispute.

predicates.civil_appeal_from_state_possession_and_d: The proceeding is a civil appeal from a decree granting the state possession of property and damages.
predicates.ruler_retained_sovereign_authority: The ruler retained sovereign authority over matters not surrendered or redistributed by the integration arrangement.
predicates.property_identified_as_private_before_gi: The ruler identified the property as private before transferring it to the recipient.
predicates.ruler_gifted_property_to_recipient: The ruler made a gift of the property to another person.
predicates.recipient_acquired_title_before_later_st: The recipient acquired title before the state later claimed the property as its own.
predicates.no_valid_divestiture_after_gift: No valid determination or other legally effective act divested the recipient of title after the gift.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal from a state decree for possession and damages, a gift remains effective against the state when the ruler retained authority, identified the property as private, transferred it to the recipient, and no valid later act divested the recipient’s title.
